source.title: An Inverse Scaling Law for CLIP Training
source.authors: Xian-Hang Li; Zeyu Wang; Cihang Xie

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses language-model scaling laws and says CLIP follows a scaling law, but its own experiments measure token-reduction effects on CLIP accuracy rather than held-out language-model loss, power-law fits, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper's own inverse-scaling results concern how changing image/text input token length affects CLIP zero-shot performance as model size changes. These do not measure the language-model loss laws in V1–V3, the architecture effect in V4, or the same power-law form specified in V5. The results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version. Scaling-law results mentioned from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains CLIP image-text models and measures how shortening image or text token sequences changes zero-shot accuracy and retrieval drops across three encoder sizes. It fits no power law and measures no held-out pretraining loss. It does no extrapolation, no compute-optimal allocation and no fixed-parameter architecture comparison. Kaplan et al. and CLIP scaling laws appear only in related work and the introduction. Larger models score higher (Tables 1, 2, 8, 11), but nothing tests whether downstream gains follow a predictable curve, so V6 and V5 are not tested either.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report an 'inverse scaling law': larger CLIP encoders can be trained with fewer image or text tokens at small performance cost. Resizing for images and syntax masking for text give the best scaling quality. They use this to build CLIPA, reaching 83.0% zero-shot ImageNet-1k with G/14 at about 33x less compute than OpenCLIP.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains contrastive image-text models and varies image/text input token lengths; it does not reproduce language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling-law methods or loss fits.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported token-reduction effect varies with the reduction strategy. The authors report that preserving more semantic information improves image-token scaling quality; syntax masking is especially effective for short text inputs. For retrieval, reducing text length to 8 or less is reported not to benefit evidently from increased model size.

fits_no_version.finding: In CLIP training, accuracy drops from shortening image or text token sequences shrink as encoder size grows (S/16 to L/16; ConvNeXt-T to B). The size of the benefit depends on the reduction strategy: resizing for images and syntax masking for text work best. For retrieval, text lengths of 8 or less show no evident benefit from larger models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger contrastive image-text encoders tolerate shorter per-sample token sequences with smaller zero-shot performance drops, depending on how tokens are removed.

record.problems: The reported results concern CLIP zero-shot accuracy and retrieval, not language-model held-out cross-entropy loss. The main ViT size comparison uses three sizes, and the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for these results.
record.rows_left_out: Many separately reported token-length, masking-strategy, robustness, retrieval, and fine-tuning results are omitted to keep the record focused and within the row limit; see Tables 9–15 and Figures 5–7. The text explicitly reports the selected numeric examples in Sections 4.1–4.3.

untested.parts: No held-out loss is measured and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute is made.
No fits on small runs are used to predict larger runs.
No loss-minimising allocation of parameters and tokens at fixed compute is reported.
No fixed-parameter comparison of depth or width; ViT vs ConvNeXt is compared on token-reduction robustness, not shape at fixed size.
No power-law form is fitted for the image-text models; only accuracy drops at three sizes are reported.
Accuracy rises with model size, but predictability of downstream performance from scale or loss is not assessed.
No fitted exponents or comparison of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The study's 'inverse scaling law' is unrelated to the loss power laws in V1–V7, despite the name; it concerns tolerance to token reduction. Model/data/schedule scaling results in Table 8 and Figure 8 (accuracy versus compute) are a few points with no fitted law, so they were not added as rows for V5 or V6. The study measures only three ViT sizes and reports no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute; power-law form and range.
Fitting power laws on small runs and testing predictions on much larger runs.
Finding loss-minimising parameter and token allocations at fixed compute, and their trends with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count assessing effects of depth, width, and other architecture details on loss.
Testing whether the same power-law form for loss holds in other modalities or training regimes.
The paper reports downstream zero-shot performance, but does not test whether it improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss as stated in this version.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and departures from a single power law.

rows.subject: CLIP S/16
rows.size_stated: ViT-S/16 vision encoder 22M parameters; text encoder 33M parameters
rows.stage_stated: Pre-training with reduced image tokens; followed by full-resolution fine-tuning
rows.operation_detail: Varied image token length using image resizing; reported performance drop from the full-resolution baseline.
rows.measure: Zero-shot top-1 accuracy performance drop relative to full-resolution baseline
rows.note: The paper compares the size-associated change in the drop: B/16 and L/16 have smaller drops at the same stated token reduction.

conditions.value: syntax masking versus truncation, block masking, and random masking

rows.baseline: Other strategies: performance drop greater than 4.0%
rows.note: The reported comparison is between token-reduction strategies, not a test of language-model loss scaling.
rows.check: Compares token-reduction strategies at fixed model size (B/16). It bears on no version, and observed/size is not the relevant axis; it is a method comparison, not a scaling result.

rows.subject: CLIP ConvNeXt-T
rows.size_stated: Similar scale to ViT-S/16; parameter count not stated
rows.stage_stated: CLIP training; same training setup as ViT with additional augmentations
rows.operation_detail: Reduced image resolution by resizing and compared zero-shot accuracy to the full-resolution baseline.
rows.measure: ImageNet-1k zero-shot top-1 accuracy drop threshold used to identify minimum input size
rows.value: Requires 112 × 112 input to meet the 1.5% performance-drop threshold
rows.note: The paper compares ConvNeXt-T with the larger ConvNeXt-B.
rows.check: The value is a selection threshold (minimum input size meeting a 1.5% drop), not a measured effect. The drop numbers are in Table 13.

rows.check: Same as r19: a threshold-based minimum input size rather than a measured drop. ConvNeXt parameter count is not stated in the text.
